questions.stem: A navigation plotter shows the boat symbol on land but the radar and depth are normal. Which input should you suspect first?
options: The GNSS position source or the chart datum
The echo sounder transducer
The VHF antenna cable
The autopilot heading input
questions.explanation: The boat symbol comes from the position source plotted on a chart. If radar and depth agree with each other and not with the plotter, suspect GNSS or the chart datum.

questions.stem: ARPA-type target tracking in chart software needs which connections?
options: An EPIRB and a SART
A weather fax and a barometer
A printer and a camera
A radar and a heading sensor
questions.explanation: The software documentation states that its ARPA target feature requires a heading sensor and a radar. Without a heading the true vectors and overlay cannot be oriented.

questions.stem: Alarm limits are CPA 0.5 nm and TCPA 10 minutes. A target closes at a relative speed of 12 knots. At about what range does a dangerous-target alarm sound for a target with a CPA of 0.3 nm?
options: About 0.5 nm
About 10 nm
About 2.0 nm
About 5 nm
questions.explanation: Both limits must be crossed. TCPA reaches 10 minutes when the distance to CPA is 12 knots × 10 ÷ 60 = 2.0 nm. So the alarm sounds at about 2 nm, which is only 10 minutes of warning.

questions.stem: A radar overlay shows the headland echo 6 degrees away from the charted point at a range of 3.0 nm. About how far is that sideways?
options: About 0.03 nm
About 0.3 nm
About 1.0 nm
About 3.0 nm
questions.explanation: Sideways offset = 3.0 × tan 6° = 3.0 × 0.105 = 0.32 nm, roughly 580 m. A heading-sensor or position problem of this size matters in a narrow channel.

questions.stem: Under NSR s. 129, what must be done when equipment fitted on or after 1 July 2002 offers alternative modes of operation?
options: The mode of operation being used must be indicated
The equipment must always be used in its default mode
Only the master may change the mode
The mode must be logged every hour
questions.explanation: Section 129 requires the mode in use to be indicated, so the watchkeeper can see at a glance what the instrument is doing.

questions.stem: What does s. 130 require when a subsystem of an integrated bridge system fails?
options: The whole system shuts down in a controlled way
A report to Transport Canada within 24 hours
The standby system takes over only after the master has approved it
Audible and visual alarms to the watch, with no knock-on failures
questions.explanation: Section 130 requires failure of any subsystem to be brought to the immediate attention of the person in charge of the deck watch by audible and visual alarms, and not to cause failure of another subsystem.

questions.stem: One part of an integrated navigation system has failed. What does s. 131 say must still be possible?
options: Operating the system only in manual mode
Using only the radar and the compass
Operating every other piece of equipment separately
Nothing more, as long as the failure is logged at once
questions.explanation: Section 131 says that in the case of a failure in one part of an integrated navigation system, it must be possible to operate every other individual piece of equipment or part of the system separately.

questions.stem: From what size does the NSR require an echo sounder, and on which smaller vessel is it also required?
options: 150 GT or more, and any passenger vessel
300 GT or more, and a towboat on a near coastal Class 1 voyage
500 GT or more, and any towboat
20 m or more, and any fishing vessel
questions.explanation: Section 110(a) requires echo-sounding equipment at 300 GT or more, and s. 125(1)(b)(i) requires it on a towboat engaged on a near coastal voyage, Class 1.

questions.stem: When a heading or track control system is used in a hazardous navigational situation, what must the person in charge of the deck watch ensure?
options: That a qualified helmsman is available at all times
That the autopilot has been reset to zero rudder first
That the master is on the bridge wing
That the autopilot is switched off
questions.explanation: Section 133(1) and (2) require immediate changeover to manual steering to be possible and the person in charge of the deck watch to ensure a qualified helmsman is available at all times. The autopilot is not forbidden.

questions.stem: How often must manual steering be tested while the heading or track control system is not in use?
options: Only at the start of each voyage
Once a week, on a set day
Once a month, during drills
Before areas needing special caution, and at least daily
questions.explanation: Section 133(4) requires manual steering to be tested before entering any area where navigation demands special caution, and at least once a day, so it is in effective operating condition.
